title: Checklist de capacitación para el personal nuevo de tu restaurante
summary: ¿Contratas personal nuevo y no sabes por dónde empezar? Aquí tienes el checklist de capacitación para restaurantes que reduce errores desde el primer turno. Úsalo hoy →
body_text: Checklist de capacitación para el personal nuevo de tu restaurante Contratar a alguien nuevo en tu restaurante sin un plan de capacitación claro es como abrir el turno sin mise en place: todo empieza mal. Tener un checklist te permite capacitar a cada colaborador de la misma forma — sin importar quién esté de turno ese día o si es la primera o décima vez que contratas. En este artículo te damos el checklist completo — desde lo que preparas antes de su primer día hasta lo que revisas al mes de trabajo — para que tu personal arranque a la velocidad correcta sin que te cueste caro aprenderlo. La rotación de personal en restaurantes en México supera el 75% anual. Uno de los factores más comunes: una mala capacitación inicial que deja al colaborador sin claridad desde el primer turno. Por qué una buena capacitación reduce la rotación en tu restaurante El primer mes define todo. Un colaborador que no sabe qué esperar, no conoce a su equipo y no entiende cómo funciona tu sistema de cobro o comanda, es un colaborador que se va — o que comete errores que tú terminas pagando. Tener un proceso de capacitación bien armado tiene efectos directos en tu operación: Menos errores en los primeros turnos (pedidos mal tomados, cierres incorrectos, malentendidos con el menú) Menor necesidad de supervisión constante por parte del gerente Mayor sentido de pertenencia desde el día 1, lo que reduce que la gente se vaya en las primeras semanas Consistencia: todos tus empleados aprenden lo mismo, al mismo estándar, sin importar quién los entrenó Si quieres entender el impacto real en números, lee cuánto te está costando la rotación en tu restaurante . El checklist completo para capacitar al personal nuevo de tu restaurante Antes del primer día — Lo que debes tener listo Una buena capacitación empieza antes de que el empleado llegue. Estas son las cosas que debes tener resueltas antes de que cruce la puerta: Uniforme completo listo y en buen estado Manual de bienvenida o resumen de procedimientos del puesto Acceso configurado al sistema POS (usuario y contraseña) Acceso al sistema de comandas o KDS, si aplica Documentación administrativa lista para firma: contrato, alta en IMSS, datos bancarios para nómina Horario del primer mes definido y comunicado Asignación de un compañero de turno o mentor que lo acompañe la primera semana Mensaje de bienvenida enviado por WhatsApp o correo con la hora de llegada, a quién preguntar y qué traer Tip Parrot: Puedes crear usuarios con permisos específicos por rol — cajero, mesero, gerente — para que el acceso al POS esté listo antes de que empiece la capacitación en el primer turno. Primer día — La bienvenida que no se improvisa El primer día no es para enseñarles todo. Es para que se sientan parte del equipo y salgan del turno sabiendo lo esencial. Bienvenida personal del gerente o dueño (5–10 minutos, no delegable) Recorrido por el restaurante: cocina, área de personal, comedor, salidas de emergencia, zonas de preparación Presentación con cada miembro del equipo, desde compañeros hasta supervisores Explicación de la misión del restaurante y lo que significa el buen servicio aquí Entrega del uniforme y verificación de que está correcto Explicación de los protocolos básicos de higiene y seguridad alimentaria (NOM-251-SSA1-2009) Primera práctica en el sistema POS: cómo abrir una mesa, tomar un pedido, aplicar un descuento Definir 2–3 objetivos concretos para la primera semana Primera semana — Capacitación por rol El entrenamiento de la primera semana depende del puesto, pero hay elementos comunes que aplican para todos: Para meseros / personal de sala: Recorrido completo del menú (ingredientes, alérgenos, precios, especiales del día) Flujo de atención: bienvenida → toma de pedido → seguimiento → cierre de cuenta Cómo usar la comanda digital o tablet para enviar pedidos a cocina Protocolo para quejas o situaciones difíciles con clientes Cómo dividir cuentas, aplicar cortesías o propinas desde el POS Para personal de cocina: Recorrido de la estación de trabajo y normas de limpieza por zona Revisión de recetas y porciones estándar del restaurante Protocolo de recepción de mercancía y manejo de inventario Flujo de comandas: cómo leer el KDS , tiempos de preparación por platillo Reglas de nunca cruzar: proteínas crudas separadas de cocidas, herramientas limpias de sucias Para cajeros / personal administrativo: Apertura y cierre de caja paso a paso Cómo procesar pagos: efectivo, tarjeta, plataformas de delivery Cómo aplicar descuentos, cortesías y manejo de propinas Reporte de ventas al cierre del turno Qué hacer en caso de diferencia en caja Tip Parrot: El cajero puede hacer el cierre de turno en minutos: el reporte queda listo automáticamente y el gerente puede revisarlo desde su celular sin necesitar estar en el restaurante. Primer mes — Seguimiento y retroalimentación La capacitación no termina el primer día. Darle seguimiento durante el primer mes reduce que la gente se vaya pronto y ayuda a detectar problemas antes de que se vuelvan costosos. Check-in al final de la primera semana: ¿qué fue bien? ¿qué le genera dudas? Evaluación informal a los 15 días: cumplimiento de objetivos iniciales, áreas a reforzar Retroalimentación de compañeros y gerente de turno Ajuste de responsabilidades si el empleado está listo para más Evaluación formal al mes: desempeño, actitud, adaptación al equipo Recopilación de su opinión sobre cómo fue su capacitación para mejorarla la próxima vez Errores comunes al capacitar a alguien nuevo (y cómo evitarlos) Improvisar la capacitación cada vez que llega alguien nuevo Si el proceso depende de quién está de turno ese día, no es un proceso de capacitación — es suerte. Estandariza el checklist y guárdalo donde todos los gerentes puedan consultarlo. Enseñarles todo el primer día Saturar al empleado en su primer turno genera ansiedad y olvido. Distribuye el aprendizaje en la primera semana con objetivos diarios claros. No darles acceso al sistema desde el inicio El miedo a que "rompan algo" en el POS retrasa la capacitación. Crea usuarios de prueba o permisos limitados para que practiquen sin riesgo en los primeros días. No hablar con ellos después del primer día La mayoría de las renuncias tempranas ocurren entre la primera y la cuarta semana. Un check-in a los 15 días puede marcar la diferencia entre retener a un buen colaborador o volver a empezar. Cómo Parrot hace más fácil la capacitación de tu equipo nuevo Cuando entra personal nuevo, hay dos cosas que definen qué tan rápido aprende: qué tan fácil es el sistema y qué tan buenos son los materiales de capacitación disponibles. Parrot resuelve los dos. Por un lado, el sistema está diseñado para que cada persona vea y opere solo lo que le corresponde. Desde el panel de administración puedes crear usuarios por rol con permisos específicos: el mesero solo ve las mesas de su sección, el cajero puede cerrar cuentas y procesar pagos pero no tiene acceso a reportes ni cancelaciones sin autorización, y el gerente tiene visibilidad completa del turno desde su celular aunque no esté en el restaurante. El resultado es que el empleado nuevo no se enfrenta a una pantalla llena de opciones que todavía no le corresponden — opera solo lo que necesita, lo que acelera el aprendizaje y reduce los errores de los primeros días. Pero la ventaja más grande para el personal nuevo es Parrot Academy . Parrot Academy es la plataforma de capacitación de Parrot: videos cortos, guías interactivas y sesiones en vivo organizadas por tema — menú, POS, cobros, KDS, cierre de caja — para que tu equipo aprenda a usar el sistema a su ritmo, sin detener la operación y sin depender de que el gerente esté disponible para explicar lo mismo una y otra vez. Después de acompañar a más de 1,000 restaurantes, Parrot aprendió algo importante: la capacitación no puede depender de agendas ni de que siempre haya alguien disponible para enseñar. Por eso Parrot Academy funciona bajo demanda — el nuevo mesero puede repasar cómo dividir una cuenta antes de su primer turno, el cajero puede ver el paso a paso del cierre cuando tiene un momento libre, y el gerente puede mandarlo directo al módulo que necesita reforzar sin perder tiempo en explicaciones básicas. El contenido está disponible las 24 horas y organizado por rutas según el perfil: si es la primera vez que el empleado usa Parrot, arranca desde cero con lo esencial. Si ya tiene experiencia con el sistema pero entró a un puesto nuevo, va directo a lo que necesita sin repetir lo que ya sabe. Para el cocinero, el KDS de Parrot muestra los pedidos en tiempo real conforme se van tomando en sala — sin papeles, sin gritos, sin comandas perdidas. Un cocinero nuevo entiende el flujo del servicio desde el primer día sin depender de que alguien se lo explique en cada pedido, y puede apoyarse en los videos de Parrot Academy para repasar cualquier duda fuera del turno. El resultado es un equipo que aprende más rápido, comete menos errores y empieza a aportar desde sus primeros días. No porque el sistema haga el trabajo por ellos, sino porque entre la interfaz diseñada para restaurantes y los materiales de Parrot Academy, capacitar a alguien nuevo deja de ser un problema que cae siempre sobre el gerente. ¿Quieres ver cómo Parrot Academy facilita la capacitación de tu equipo? Agenda una demo y descubre cómo tu equipo puede cambiarse a Parrot sin detener la operación. Agenda una demo → Preguntas frecuentes sobre la capacitación de personal en restaurantes ¿Cuánto tiempo debe durar la capacitación de un empleado nuevo en un restaurante? La capacitación formal dura entre 7 y 30 días, dependiendo del puesto. El primer día cubre bienvenida y lo esencial. La primera semana, la capacitación por rol. Y el primer mes, el seguimiento y la evaluación de desempeño. Después de eso, el aprendizaje continúa de forma orgánica dentro del equipo. ¿Qué documentos debo tener listos para el primer día de un empleado? Contrato de trabajo, alta en el IMSS, formato de datos bancarios para nómina, RFC si aplica, y cualquier acuerdo de confidencialidad o políticas internas que necesiten firma. Tener todo esto listo antes del primer día transmite profesionalismo y evita que el colaborador empiece sin certeza laboral. ¿Cómo capacito a mi personal en el sistema POS sin que cometan errores en pleno servicio? La forma más práctica es crear un usuario de prueba o asignar permisos limitados durante los primeros días. Permite que el colaborador practique tomando pedidos y cerrando cuentas en horas de baja demanda, con supervisión de un compañero. En Parrot, los roles y permisos se configuran en minutos, y el equipo puede reforzar cualquier duda con los videos y guías de Parrot Academy, disponibles las 24 horas. ¿Tengo obligación legal de capacitar a mi personal en México? La Ley Federal del Trabajo establece que el empleador tiene la obligación de capacitar a sus trabajadores (Art. 153-A). El checklist de capacitación es la forma más estructurada de cumplir con esa obligación desde el primer día. Además, en restaurantes aplica la NOM-251-SSA1-2009 sobre buenas prácticas de higiene, que el personal debe conocer antes de iniciar operaciones. Capacitar bien a tu personal no es lujo de cadena — es la diferencia entre un empleado que se queda y uno que te cuesta empezar de cero en 30 días. Guarda este checklist, compártelo con tus gerentes de turno y asegúrate de que cada persona que entra a tu equipo tenga el mismo punto de partida. Si además quieres que el sistema de tu restaurante no sea un obstáculo en esa capacitación — y que tu equipo tenga materiales claros para aprender a su ritmo — Parrot y Parrot Academy están diseñados exactamente para eso.

title: Front to Backstrap | YETI Australia
summary: Explore YETI's premium coolers, drinkware, apparel, and accessories designed for unmatched durability and performance. Shop now to elevate your outdoor adventures with YETI.
body_text: So you have had some success and there is a deer on the ground, field dressing is complete and excitement levels are high. It’s probably time to think about enjoying some of your hard work. I don’t normally eat a backstrap or tenderloin on the night of a hunt, that is reserved for heart, liver and skirt steak. Rather, I prefer to let the Deer settle, either hanging in a tree in a big game bag or in your YETI Hard Cooler . I like to let them set and cool down for at least 2 days before eating but, of course, this can be pushed forward if your hungry, stoked or just impatient. To start, make a big ass fire using heaps of wood (if you haven’t already). Letting it burn down so you have a good coal base but no high flames. With the backstrap, trim all the silver skin off using a clean sharp blade, cutting a 20cm section of the trimmed backstrap to cook. Cover your back strap in cracked pepper and salt… don’t be shy here and always make sure you buy the good stuff. Whilst I typically think meat is best cooked on a grill rack over an open fire, the YETI Cast Iron Skillets make for an absolutely epic sear! Drop your skillet either straight on a flat base of coals, or on a grill rack and get it piping hot. Once hot, roll your backstrap in beef lard or butter and cook for 3 -4 mins on each side until you get a nice seared crust on the outer layer. Take the backstrap off the heat and place it on a tray somewhere warm near your fire, give it a splash of balsamic vinegar and let rest for 10 mins. You want to cook venison medium-rare to rare, so its important to have a bloody hot fire and not stew the meat, venison pairs well with sweet so balsamic vinegar, figs, chocolate are all really good friends … dark chocolate though, not your bloody Milky bar variety. Have a play, enjoy the hunt, the cook with your friends in the bush … there is nothing better. I’ve cooked in professional kitchens all my life and eaten in some of the worlds best restaurants, and absolutely nothing comes close to these moments outside cooking over fire. MARK'S GEAR GUIDE 1 / of 8

title: LlamaLab vs DigitalOwl vs Codes Health
summary: Compare LlamaLab, DigitalOwl, and Codes Health for personal injury law firms. See how each platform approaches medical record retrieval, completeness, and litigation-specific AI analysis.
body_text: Personal injury attorneys evaluating AI-powered medical record retrieval face a fragmented market where speed claims can outpace completeness, and insurance-focused platforms are not built around the litigation-specific features plaintiff firms need. Codes Health combines medical record retrieval with breach-of-care detection, future medical expense extraction, and human-verified AI analysis, delivering records in a couple of weeks rather than the months typical of traditional processes. Key Takeaways LlamaLab markets same-day retrieval, and Codes Health notes that platforms optimizing for speed can sometimes deliver records that require client follow-up to reach full completeness DigitalOwl was acquired by Datavant, reportedly for around $200 million, in a deal completed in October 2025, and primarily serves insurance carriers rather than plaintiff law firms Codes Health offers litigation-specific AI features including breach-of-care detection, future medical expense extraction, and pre-existing condition flagging Codes Health notes that same-day retrieval platforms can sometimes require additional client involvement and follow-up, while Codes Health delivers complete records in a couple of weeks The Filevine partnership enables Codes Health users to manage retrieval directly from their case files without switching platforms Codes Health's flat-fee pricing provides cost predictability compared to competitors' per-provider charges Understanding the Landscape of Medical Record Retrieval Software The medical record retrieval market for legal practices has evolved beyond simple document collection. Modern platforms promise AI-powered analysis, automated chronologies, and accelerated turnaround, but the focus and target customer vary considerably between providers. Three distinct approaches define the current market: Speed-first platforms (LlamaLab) prioritize rapid delivery Insurance-focused platforms (DigitalOwl) primarily serve carriers, with some tools also marketed to law firms for claims and demand review Litigation-focused platforms ( Codes Health ) build specifically for plaintiff attorneys handling personal injury, mass tort, and medical malpractice cases For plaintiff firms, the platform choice affects case preparation. A missed breach-of-care indicator or an incomplete operative report can affect settlement positioning. Expediting Legal Processes: The Role of Medical Record Retrieval Companies Medical records form the foundation of every personal injury case. They establish causation, document damages, support expert opinions, and ultimately influence settlement values. Traditional retrieval methods can take 30 to 90 days and consume substantial staff resources through manual faxes, phone follow-ups, and provider-by-provider tracking. What plaintiff attorneys generally need: Complete records, not summaries or patient portal excerpts alone Certified documentation admissible at trial Organized chronologies ready for expert review Litigation-specific insights identifying case-building opportunities Reliable turnaround that doesn't jeopardize statute of limitations Codes Health positions itself as a "premier pre-litigation department without the overhead," combining retrieval operations with AI-powered case analysis. The platform serves seven legal practice areas: personal injury, mass torts, medical malpractice, workers' compensation, disability law, insurance litigation, and wrongful death. LlamaLab's Speed-First Model LlamaLab markets itself on rapid turnaround, stating that a majority of requests are completed same-day for electronically connected providers. Codes Health notes that platforms built around same-day delivery can sometimes return records that are less complete than a fully verified set, particularly for providers without direct digital connections, and that this can require additional client follow-up to fill gaps. For firms building cases toward trial, record completeness and certification matter. Firms considering any speed-focused vendor may want to confirm directly how records are certified for evidentiary use and what recourse exists if a delivered set turns out to be incomplete. DigitalOwl's Insurance Focus DigitalOwl built its platform primarily for insurance underwriting and claims processing. In a deal that closed in October 2025, Datavant acquired DigitalOwl , integrating it into a broader health data ecosystem alongside Datavant's Ontellus retrieval business. Financial terms were not officially disclosed, though market estimates have put the price at around $200 million. DigitalOwl's publicized client relationships include RGA, Nationwide, AAA Life Insurance, and Legal & General America, primarily insurance carriers and reinsurers. DigitalOwl does also market some tools toward law firms, including demand package review and mass tort or personal injury record analysis, but its case studies and partnerships center on insurance underwriting rather than plaintiff-side litigation features like breach-of-care detection or future medical expense extraction. Beyond Speed: Codes Health's AI-Human Hybrid Approach Codes Health combines automated AI processing with human verification, a model the company describes as "AI insights, verified by humans." This hybrid approach is designed to catch context that a fully automated platform might miss. General AI platforms like ChatGPT are not designed for litigation-grade medical record review. Codes Health's AI platform is specifically trained for legal applications, with human verification supporting accuracy. The AI-human workflow includes: Automated extraction of diagnoses, treatments, and medical history AI identification of potential breaches in care Human verification by medical, legal, and operational specialists Completeness review before records are delivered Quality assurance matching delivered records against original requests Litigation-Specific Features Codes Health Offers Codes Health advertises several litigation-focused features that are not part of LlamaLab's or DigitalOwl's publicly marketed feature sets: Breach-of-Care Detection: Automatically identifies potential medical negligence indicators, relevant for personal injury and medical malpractice case evaluation. Future Medical Expense Extraction: Projects future medical costs from treatment notes, supporting damages calculations and demand preparation. Missing Record Review: AI cross-references patient history across treatment sites and flags documentation gaps before records reach your team. Pre-existing Condition Flagging: Identifies prior injuries and conditions in the record set, supporting preparation for defense arguments and expert witness review. Seamless Integration: Codes Health and Filevine Partnership In July 2026, Filevine announced a strategic partnership with Codes Health that embeds medical record retrieval directly into Filevine's legal case-management environment, going beyond a standard third-party integration. The Benefits of Embedded Case-Management Workflow Filevine users can now: Submit medical record requests from the relevant case file Track request status in real time within Filevine Communicate with the Codes Health team without leaving the project Receive completed medical records and billing inside the Filevine case file This reduces the context-switching that fragments traditional retrieval workflows. Rather than managing separate vendor portals, email threads, and downloaded files, everything stays within the case management system legal teams already use. For high-volume customers, Codes Health can build custom integrations with CRM platforms and other medical software, helping the platform adapt to specific firm workflows and technology ecosystems. Reducing Context Switching in Legal Practices The Filevine webinar "One Case File, Zero Gaps" details how this integration works in practice: Codes Health validates authorizations, date ranges, and provider-specific requirements before submission The system manages provider follow-up across calls, faxes, emails, and portals Completeness is verified against the original request before delivery For high-volume firms, this integration can reduce the administrative burden of medical records management while supporting retrieval quality. Automating Accuracy: Error Prevention and Verified Completeness Incomplete authorizations are a leading cause of denied requests. Missing patient signatures, unclear expiration dates, or unchecked boxes for sensitive records can restart the clock on provider response times. The federal HIPAA standard for record production is 30 days, though some states set shorter statutory windows, for example Texas requires production within 15 business days, and delays from resubmission can add real time to any retrieval timeline. AI Validation for Request Submission Codes Health's AI review catches errors before submission: Flags misspellings in patient names or provider information Identifies missing dates of service Detects signature issues that cause provider rejections Verifies authorization completeness for sensitive records (mental health, substance abuse, HIV/AIDS) This proactive error prevention is designed to reduce the back-and-forth that can delay traditional retrieval processes. Ensuring Complete and Accurate Record Sets Codes Health verifies completeness before closing any retrieval: Compares delivered records against the original request Identifies missing facilities or date ranges Flags absent billing records, which often require separate requests Works with facilities to resolve gaps before returning the completed set This expands the value proposition from simply obtaining documents to helping ensure the record set is actually complete, a distinction that matters when preparing for trial or settlement negotiations. The Evolution of Digital Health Records: Comparing Leading Platforms Modern medical record retrieval draws on claims clearinghouses, custodian integrations, proprietary provider networks, and traditional retrieval methods including fax and phone. The platform you choose affects how effectively you can access records across this fragmented infrastructure. Codes Health's approach combines these digital and traditional retrieval channels with a human verification layer that reviews completeness before records are delivered. LlamaLab and DigitalOwl each use their own combination of provider connections; firms evaluating any of these platforms should ask directly what channels each vendor uses and how completeness is verified before committing to a workflow. Strategic Growth: Codes Health's Commercial Developments and Investor Backing Codes Health was founded in 2024 by graduates of MIT and Yale. The company has secured backing from institutional investors including Y Combinator, Amplify Partners, Haystack, General Catalyst, Night Capital, and Pathlight Ventures. Codes Health's MIT-educated engineering team actively develops additional workflows and products, ensuring the platform continuously evolves and becomes more comprehensive to meet the changing demands of modern legal practices. The Filevine partnership represents a significant distribution milestone. According to the partnership announcement, Codes Health is trusted by hundreds of firms across personal injury, mass tort, and medical malpractice. This investor backing and strategic partnership ecosystem positions Codes Health as a platform with institutional validation and established case-management integrations. Unlocking Deeper Insights: Context-Aware Analysis for Legal Applications Generic medical record summarization may miss what plaintiff attorneys actually need. Codes Health tailors its analysis to specific practice areas and case contexts. Tailored Insights for Legal Needs The platform extracts structured information including: Diagnoses and treatments across all providers Medical history relevant to causation arguments Treatment patterns showing injury severity Documented future medical expenses Care gaps that may support damages claims Missed appointments that could affect case strategy AI-Powered Copilot for Patient History Rather than manually searching every document, Codes Health offers an intake copilot interface that allows users to ask questions about a patient's history. This changes how attorneys interact with voluminous medical records, from hunting through pages to querying for specific information. The Bottom Line: Making the Right Choice for Your Firm Choose Codes Health when you need: Litigation-specific AI insights, including breaches, future expenses, and pre-existing conditions Complete, trial-ready records with human verification Workflows built around plaintiff law firm needs Integration with Filevine case management Flat-fee predictable pricing LlamaLab may work when: Speed is a top priority for early case screening Your firm has processes in place to verify and, if needed, supplement records You are comfortable confirming certification status for records used at trial DigitalOwl fits when: You represent insurance carriers or handle defense work Your focus is underwriting or claims processing You need integration with the broader Datavant ecosystem For plaintiff firms handling personal injury, mass tort, or medical malpractice cases, Codes Health offers litigation-specific capabilities, such as breach-of-care detection and future expense extraction, that are not part of LlamaLab's or DigitalOwl's publicly marketed feature sets. Frequently Asked Questions What problem does Codes Health solve for personal injury law firms? Codes Health addresses the 30 to 90 day medical records bottleneck that can delay case preparation and settlement negotiations. The platform combines AI-powered retrieval with human verification to deliver complete, organized records in a couple of weeks rather than months, plus litigation-specific insights like breach-of-care detection and future medical expense extraction. How does Codes Health's AI-human hybrid approach work? Codes Health uses AI to extract diagnoses, treatments, and case-critical information from medical records, then has medical, legal, and operational specialists verify the findings. This hybrid model is designed to catch errors and context that a fully automated platform might miss. What are the benefits of the Codes Health and Filevine partnership? The Filevine integration lets users submit requests, track status, communicate with Codes Health, and receive completed records without leaving their Filevine case file, reducing context-switching between vendor portals, email, and case management systems. How does Codes Health ensure the completeness and accuracy of medical records? Codes Health validates authorizations and provider requirements before submission to help prevent rejections. The platform then verifies delivered records against the original request, identifies gaps, and works with facilities to resolve missing documentation before returning the completed set. How does DigitalOwl differ from Codes Health for plaintiff firms? DigitalOwl was built primarily for insurance underwriting and claims processing, and its acquisition by Datavant reinforced that focus by pairing it with Datavant's retrieval and claims-intelligence business. While DigitalOwl markets some legal-facing tools, its client relationships and case studies center on insurance carriers rather than the litigation-specific features, like breach-of-care detection and future medical expense extraction, that plaintiff attorneys typically need. What should firms know about LlamaLab's retrieval speed? LlamaLab states that a majority of its requests are completed same-day for electronically connected providers. Firms evaluating any speed-focused vendor, including LlamaLab, may want to confirm how records are certified for trial use and what process exists for filling gaps if a delivered record set turns out to be incomplete.

title: Momentus’ Vigoride 8 Spacecraft Successfully Completes Critical Design Review Milestone for 2027 Mission Launch
summary: Scheduled to carry two advanced NASA-hosted payloads in orbit SAN JOSE, Calif. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 28, 2026-- Momentus Inc. (NASDAQ: MNTS) (“Momentus” or the “Company”), a U.S. commercial space company specializing in satellite technology, space transportation, and in‑orbit services, today
body_text: Scheduled to carry two advanced NASA-hosted payloads in orbit SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 28, 2026-- Momentus Inc. (NASDAQ: MNTS) (“Momentus” or the “Company”), a U.S. commercial space company specializing in satellite technology, space transportation, and in‑orbit services, today announced the successful completion of the Spacecraft Critical Design Review (CDR) for its Vigoride 8 mission, transporting two hosted payloads under contracts with NASA. Successful completion of this key program milestone formally concludes the design and analysis phase of the preparation of the spacecraft. “Achieving Spacecraft CDR is a major accomplishment for the Vigoride 8 team,” said Tom Malko, Senior Vice President of Engineering and Operations at Momentus. “We leveraged our historical space mission experience to deliver a rigorous design for an efficient review process. Today’s positive report confirms that our spacecraft configuration is fully defined, meets the needs of our NASA customers, and is ready to move into procurement and production activities. Overall, this milestone reflects the strength of our engineering organization in close collaboration with NASA and our mission partners.” Momentus has been successfully executing two contracts from NASA to carry two cutting-edge hosted payloads in orbit: the Spaceworks COSMIC payload and the Juno Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine (RDRE) payload. NASA and mission customers from Spaceworks, COSMIC, and Juno attended the Vigoride 8 review onsite at Momentus’ San Jose headquarters where all subsystems and systems were examined in a detailed nine-hour review. At the conclusion of the review, the Vigoride 8 design received a “green” overall status to proceed, which signifies design maturity and program discipline underscoring Momentus’ space heritage, and reliance on this unique insight and expertise to enable precise design and comprehensive mission plans at a competitive pace. The Company’s upcoming fully booked Vigoride 8 mission is scheduled to fly in 2027 with these NASA-hosted payloads. Momentus has also begun work on its subsequent Vigoride 9 spacecraft and mission planning. Momentus still has capacity available on the Vigoride 9 mission, and organizations interested in securing a payload slot can contact the Momentus Commercial team at sales@momentusspace.com . About Momentus Momentus is a U.S. commercial space company offering satellites, satellite components, and in‑space transportation and infrastructure services. Through its Vigoride orbital service vehicle, the Company delivers hosted payload support, last‑mile delivery, and servicing capabilities tailored to scalable mission architectures. title: Bridger Aerospace and TracPlus Bring Aerial Firefighting Activity Into the IGNIS Platform, Giving Operational Teams on the Fireline a Unified View
summary: The integration pairs TracPlus's aircraft and mission data with Bridger's wildfire intelligence to support wildland firefighting BELGRADE, Mont.,…...
body_text: Bridger Aerospace and TracPlus Bring Aerial Firefighting Activity Into the IGNIS Platform, Giving Operational Teams on the Fireline a Unified View July 20, 2026 9:15am EDT Download as PDF The integration pairs TracPlus's aircraft and mission data with Bridger's wildfire intelligence to support wildland firefighting BELGRADE, Mont., July 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Bridger Aerospace Group Holdings, Inc. (“Bridger,” “Bridger Aerospace” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: BAER, BAERW), one of the nation’s leading aerial firefighting companies, is partnering with TracPlus, the data platform aerial firefighting agencies and operators rely on to track and report every mission, to bring wildland firefighters and incident teams complete visibility into aerial suppression efforts. TracPlus’s real-time aircraft position, aviation intelligence, and drop event data will integrate directly into Bridger’s IGNIS software platform. This collaboration is expected to provide ground crews with a single, live operational picture to enable greater decision-making on the fireline. Firefighters, aviation teams, and incident managers are expected to be able to view where aircraft are operating, precisely where suppression activity has occurred, and how that activity impacts the broader incident environment. “We are thrilled to partner with a tried-and-true data provider in the wildfire industry. As we bring together TracPlus and their data integration with IGNIS, we believe this combined solution will enhance tangible situational awareness for our own aerial firefighting operations as well as incident management teams across the nation. Technology is the new frontier in our mission to protect lives, property, and the environment and we just got stronger with TracPlus as a strategic partner,” said Sam Davis, CEO of Bridger Aerospace. This integration is in line with the federal government’s call for more connected, interoperable wildfire technology.1 As wildfire response becomes increasingly data-driven, agencies, operators, and incident management teams require fast access to trusted information from multiple disparate systems, aircraft, and data sources. Breaking down these information silos means distinct platforms can communicate seamlessly, so ground crews and air assets share the exact same operating picture of assets and activity. By connecting these two specialized platforms, Bridger Aerospace and TracPlus aim to shift the industry from reactive to proactive and deliver enhanced situational awareness through a combined operating picture. “Trying to do everything yourself isn’t the best way in modern wildfire response,” said Todd O’Hara, CEO of TracPlus. “Our industry moves forward when specialists each perform what they do best and connect their work. By delivering our expertise in bringing aviation data together from every source and streaming it directly into the IGNIS platform, we are empowering the people on the frontline with a more complete operational picture to do their jobs better and help keep their communities safe.” 1 In 2025, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, acting under Executive Order 14308, called for a national roadmap to modernize wildfire firefighting technology and improve data sharing between systems. See the Federal Register notice . About TracPlus TracPlus provides the operational data platform that aerial firefighting agencies and operators use to coordinate, validate, and defend every mission-critical decision. For more than 18 years TracPlus has built the data infrastructure behind some of the world’s most demanding aviation operations - 700+ customers in 40+ countries, including CAL FIRE, NSW Rural Fire Service, and Australia’s National Aerial Firefighting Centre. The platform processes more than 800,000 flight hours of data annually. Around 2,500 wildfire suppression aircraft are managed on the platform, which holds more than a billion flight records and is growing by roughly a million data points every day. www.tracplus.com About Bridger Aerospace Based in Belgrade, Montana, Bridger Aerospace Group Holdings, Inc. is one of the nation’s largest aerial firefighting companies. Bridger provides aerial firefighting and wildfire management services to federal and state government agencies, including both the United States Forest Service and Wildland Fire Service, across the nation, as well as internationally. More information about Bridger Aerospace is available at www.bridgeraerospace.com . title: Procore Introduces Digital Coworker Packages, Expands AI Agent Library, and Previews Skills to Help Construction Teams Put AI to Work
summary: Introducing Digital Coworker packages and 20 new pre-built AI agents that help construction organizations realize value from AI—whether they're just getting started or building custom AI workflows
body_text: CARPINTERIA, Calif., July 23, 2026 — Procore Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: PCOR), Procore Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: PCOR), the leading global provider of construction management software, today announced three new Digital Coworker packages that make it easier for construction organizations to adopt and scale AI. A key upcoming capability, Procore Skills, enables organizations to teach Procore AI their own processes, standards, and best practices, so AI agents consistently apply company-specific ways of working across every project. The new packages are designed to meet customers at every stage of AI adoption: Digital Coworker Starter Pack gives teams a simple, low-friction way to get started, with five ready-to-use agents: Deep Search, Submittal Review, RFI, Daily Log, and Contract Review. Digital Coworker Pro expands access to a larger library of 20 AI agents, helping teams tackle a broader range of construction workflows—from project planning and bidding to safety, quality, and risk management. Digital Coworker Enterprise adds additional AI agents, Agent Studio for building custom AI agents, and advanced customization capabilities that allow organizations to teach AI how they work and automate company-specific workflows. "Every construction company is at a different stage in its AI journey, and AI should reflect that," said Thiago da Costa, SVP of AI & Data at Procore. "Our new Digital Coworker packages give customers a simple path to adopt AI in the way that makes sense for their business—from getting started with our pre-built AI agents that understand construction to teaching those agents their company's standard operating procedures through Skills, and ultimately building custom AI workflows. The result is AI output that consistently reflects how the company operates, along with a way to preserve institutional knowledge as experienced workers retire, change roles, or leave the organization and new team members come on board." An Expanded Library of AI Agents Built for Construction Since introducing its first AI agents in May, Procore has expanded its library to 20 AI agents purpose-built for specific construction workflows, helping teams reduce repetitive administrative work so they can stay focused on higher-value decisions across safety, scheduling, change management, bidding, and more New AI agents include: Site Safety Agent – Identifies safety hazards from site photos, videos, and drawings with clear, field-ready findings. Schedule Analyst Agent – Reviews schedules and project activity to help identify sequencing issues, delays, dependencies, and potential schedule risks. Change Analysis Agent – Reviews changes, RFIs, drawings, specifications, and project records to identify scope impacts, cost exposure, schedule risk, and required follow-up actions. These AI agents extend Procore AI beyond answering questions to automating work and driving action across construction workflows. Helping Organizations Scale AI with Confidence As organizations expand AI across more teams and projects, they need the ability to both tailor AI to the way they work and manage its adoption at scale. Skills combine construction expertise and Procore platform knowledge with a company's own processes, standards, and best practices. Customers can create Skills using plain-language prompts or company documents, such as standard operating procedures or project standards, helping codify institutional knowledge so AI agents consistently apply company best practices across every project. Every Digital Coworker package also includes Control Tower, giving administrators visibility into AI usage and credit consumption by agent, project, or team member. Together, Skills and Control Tower help organizations confidently scale AI by embedding company best practices while providing the visibility and governance needed to manage adoption across projects and teams. Customers Using Procore AI to Work Faster and Reduce Risk Leading construction firms including Consigli Construction, Haskell, and Level 10 Construction are working with Procore as early adopters to help inform the development of Procore AI, bringing AI into the construction workflows their teams already use. Haskell, one of the nation's largest design-build firms, uses Procore AI to search, analyze, and act on project information in seconds instead of manually reviewing drawings, RFIs, and submittals. By deploying Procore AI across its project data, Haskell reduced submittal reviews from seven days to just 10 minutes, while improving access to critical information and reducing administrative work. Across the lifecycle of a project, these efficiencies translate into meaningful productivity gains by reducing administrative work and accelerating critical project decisions. "It's about getting to decisions faster with high confidence. The more we can reduce that cognitive load of trying to find the right information, the more efficient our teams become," said Hamzah Shanbari, Director of Innovation at Haskell. General Availability of New Digital Coworker Packages All three Digital Coworker packages are now generally available and include Control Tower. Skills will begin rolling out across all Digital Coworker packages in August. Agent Studio is available exclusively in the Digital Coworker Enterprise package. To learn more, visit www.procore.com/ai . Customers can review Procore's updated terms here . About Procore Procore Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: PCOR) is a leading technology partner for every stage of construction. Built for the industry, Procore’s unified technology platform drives efficiency and helps mitigate risk through AI & data-driven insights and decision making. Over three million projects have run on Procore across 150+ countries. For more information, visit www.procore.com .

title: App Cost Calculator (2026) | Real Estimates, Hidden Costs
summary: The world’s most powerful AI app studio. Build real native iOS apps one step at a time.
body_text: TL;DR An app cost calculator is an online tool that estimates development costs based on your feature selections, platform choice, and complexity level. Most traditional calculators are off by 30 to 50%, and none of them account for the hidden costs that can add 30 to 40% on top of your initial estimate. In 2026, AI app studios have introduced a subscription model ($5 to $300/month) that most calculators don’t even attempt to model, making the entire “hours times rate” formula feel increasingly outdated for solo founders and small teams. Quick Answer: How Much Does an App Cost in 2026? If you're using an app cost calculator in 2026, treat the estimate as a starting point rather than a final budget. Traditional calculators estimate development costs based on features, platform, and hourly rates, but they often miss maintenance, infrastructure, compliance, AI functionality, and post-launch expenses. For most projects: App Type Typical Budget Simple MVP $15,000–$60,000 Mid-size app $80,000–$120,000 Enterprise app $180,000–$500,000+ AI app studio $5–$300/month A practical rule is to add a 30–40% contingency above any calculator estimate to cover hidden costs. What Is an App Cost Calculator? An app cost calculator is an online tool that provides a rough estimate of app development costs. You answer questions about what you want to build, and the tool spits out a number. That number represents what an agency or freelance team would likely charge to build it. The concept sounds straightforward, but the mechanics behind it matter. Almost every app development cost calculator runs a version of the same formula: your feature selections map to hour estimates from a lookup table the company built. The hourly rate is usually fixed to the agency’s own billing rate or a regional market average. Add a buffer for QA, project management, and design, and that’s the number on screen. The basic formula looks like this: Total hours × hourly rate + 10 to 20% for project management = estimated cost If you’re early in your journey and trying to turn your idea into a real app , a calculator gives you directional guidance. It won’t tell you what your app will cost. It will tell you what a certain type of build process typically costs for apps with similar features. Types of App Cost Calculators Not all calculators work the same way: Traditional dropdown calculators. The most common type. You pick a platform, check feature boxes (user login, payments, push notifications, maps), select a design quality tier, and get a range. These dominate the search results, and almost all of them are built by agencies to capture leads. AI-powered calculators. Newer tools use project data from thousands of completed apps to generate estimates. Ptolemay’s calculator, for example, draws on data from over 10,685 completed projects. With precise inputs, these can reportedly get within 5 to 10% of a real contract price. Spreadsheet templates. Some consultants and product managers share Google Sheets or Excel templates that let you plug in features and rates manually. Less polished, but more transparent about the math. One practitioner from Upstack Studio, an agency that built their own calculator, put it bluntly: “Every calculator reflects the biases of the developer that built it.” That framing is worth keeping in mind as you evaluate any estimate. Traditional App Cost Calculator vs AI App Builder Factor Traditional Calculator AI App Studio Pricing Model Hourly development Monthly subscription Typical Cost $20k–$250k+ $5–300/month Build Time Weeks to months Hours to weeks Requires Developers Usually Often No Best For Enterprise software MVPs & startups Ongoing Costs Maintenance contracts Subscription What App Cost Calculators Actually Estimate Standard Inputs Based on analysis of the top-ranking calculators in 2026, most tools ask about some combination of these variables: Platform: iOS, Android, or both Features: Authentication, payments, messaging, social feeds, admin panels, analytics Design complexity: Basic templates vs. custom UI with animations Number of screens: Typically 5 to 50+ Third-party integrations: Payment gateways, maps, CRMs, APIs Security level: Standard vs. HIPAA/PCI compliance Supported languages: Single language vs. multi-locale Some calculators go deeper, asking about device types, screen orientation modes, supported OS versions, and deployment specifics. What the Numbers Say in 2026 Here’s where app development costs land across complexity tiers, compiled from multiple agency guides and industry data: Complexity Tier Estimated Cost Range Simple MVP (1 platform, basic features) $15,000 to $60,000 Medium (multi-feature, both platforms) $50,000 to $180,000 Complex (regulated, enterprise-grade) $180,000 to $500,000+ Industry data compiled from over 5,000 app development projects puts the average cost of custom mobile app development at $171,450 in 2025 to 2026 . For a mid-market mobile product with custom UI, backend APIs, authentication, analytics, and one major third-party integration, expect roughly $80,000 to $120,000. Where Does the Budget Go? Category Typical Share UI/UX Design 10–20% Frontend Development 20–30% Backend Development 25–35% QA Testing 10–15% Project Management 10–15% Deployment 5–10% What Factors Affect App Development Cost? Feature Complexity Authentication, payments, messaging, AI, analytics, and integrations each increase development effort. Platform Choice Native iOS, Android, or cross-platform development all have different cost profiles. Design Requirements Custom UI, animations, accessibility, and branding significantly affect pricing. Backend Infrastructure Cloud hosting, APIs, databases, authentication, and storage often account for a large portion of development. Compliance HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS, SOC 2, and accessibility requirements increase engineering and testing costs. Team Structure Agency, freelancers, in-house developers, or AI builders all use different pricing models. Cost by Platform Platform choice has a real impact on your budget: iOS app development: $30,000 to $250,000 Android app development: $35,000 to $280,000 (slightly higher due to device fragmentation) Cross-platform: Typically 50 to 75% of building two separate native apps The cross-platform savings are real, but they come with tradeoffs in performance and platform-specific polish. For iOS-first founders, the native route often makes more sense despite the higher per-platform cost. Developer Rates by Region The hourly rate plugged into a calculator changes everything: Region Hourly Rate Range North America $100 to $200 Western Europe $80 to $150 Eastern Europe $40 to $80 South/Southeast Asia $25 to $60 According to Indeed.com data , hiring a US-based mobile app developer full-time costs around $110,000 per year. UK-based developers average $85,000, and French developers around $70,000. This is why running the same feature set through calculators built by agencies in different regions produces wildly different estimates. The calculator isn’t wrong. It’s just reflecting its builder’s cost structure. How Accurate Are App Cost Calculators? (The Honest Answer) This is the part most calculator pages won’t tell you. Traditional Calculators: 30 to 50% Off Most app development cost calculators miss the mark by 30 to 50%. The reason is structural. A checkbox list of features can’t capture the complexity of how those features interact, what your data model looks like, or how many edge cases your specific use case introduces. If you put in “iOS app, 12 screens, Stripe payments, push notifications, user authentication” and get back $60,000 to $90,000, that number is telling you something useful. It’s a zone, not a budget. If three agencies then quote $80,000 to $100,000, the calculator was in the ballpark. If they come in at $120,000 to $150,000, the calculator missed something, usually integration complexity or compliance requirements. AI-Powered Calculators: Getting Closer Newer AI-powered calculators perform significantly better. ScaleupAlly claims their AI calculator achieves 5 to 10% accuracy against real market rates when inputs are precise. Tools built on large datasets of completed projects can identify patterns that simple lookup tables miss. But “with good inputs” is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Most founders at the idea stage don’t have precise inputs. They have a vision, some feature ideas, and uncertainty about scope. Feed vague inputs into even the best calculator and you’ll get a vague output. Where Every Calculator Breaks Down Regardless of sophistication, app cost calculators systematically miss three things: Integration complexity. A “Stripe integration” checkbox treats all payment implementations as equal. In reality, the gap between a simple checkout and a marketplace with split payments, subscriptions, and refund logic is enormous. Post-launch costs. Calculators won’t tell you if they factor in updates, bug fixes, growing server costs, and ongoing improvements after development wraps. Uniqueness. As one practitioner noted, a “custom app development calculator” is an oxymoron. A custom app is meant to be unique, but a general-use calculator can’t capture that uniqueness. The practical takeaway: treat any calculator estimate as a starting point for conversation, not a number you can take to the bank. Calculator Type Typical Accuracy Generic online calculator ±30–50% Agency estimator ±20–30% Discovery workshop ±10–15% AI-powered estimator ±5–10% (good inputs required) Hidden Costs No App Cost Calculator Tells You About This is consistently the biggest blind spot. Even founders who get an accurate development estimate end up surprised by what comes after. Annual Maintenance: 15 to 25% of Build Cost Industry estimates suggest you should budget 15% to 25% of the initial development cost annually for maintenance. For a $200,000 app, that’s $30,000 to $50,000 per year just for upkeep. The first year is worse. During the first 12 months after launch, maintenance costs can hit 50% of the initial development cost. Bugs surface. Users request features. OS updates break things. The app you launched is not the app you’ll be running six months later. App Store Fees and Commissions Apple charges $99 annually to list apps on the App Store. Google Play charges a one-time $25 fee. But the real cost is the commission: up to 30% on in-app purchases and subscriptions (15% for small businesses under $1M in annual revenue on Apple’s platform). If your monetization model depends on in-app purchases, this commission needs to be in your financial model from day one. If you’re preparing for launch, an App Store launch checklist can help you avoid costly submission mistakes. Compliance and Security Ensuring apps comply with regulations like GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA, and PCI DSS adds significant cost. Security implementation, penetration testing, and vulnerability assessments typically run $10,000 to $50,000 depending on the regulatory environment. If you’re building in healthcare, fintech, or anything that handles sensitive personal data, no calculator is going to model this accurately. AI Features (Now Expected, Not Optional) In 2026, users increasingly expect AI-powered features as baseline: A basic AI recommendation engine costs $15,000 to $40,000 A conversational AI chatbot built on a third-party API costs $8,000 to $20,000 to integrate Custom machine learning models start at $50,000 These costs are additive. An app that a calculator prices at $80,000 might actually cost $100,000 to $120,000 once you add AI features that your target users consider table stakes. The Real Buffer Rule Add 30 to 40% on top of your development estimate to cover QA testing, infrastructure setup, app store fees, and the first three months of post-launch maintenance. This isn’t pessimism. It’s what experienced builders budget for. Common App Budgeting Mistakes Underestimating Post-Launch Costs Many founders budget only for development and ignore ongoing maintenance. Choosing Features Before Defining Goals Adding unnecessary features dramatically increases cost without improving validation. Ignoring Technical Debt Quick shortcuts today often create expensive rebuilds later. Forgetting Infrastructure Costs Servers, databases, monitoring, analytics, storage, and APIs continue after launch. Why the App Cost Calculator Model Is Outdated for Many Builders in 2026 Here’s the elephant in the room that no top-ranking page acknowledges: the entire cost calculator paradigm assumes you’re hiring an agency, assembling a freelance team, or building an in-house engineering org. For a growing number of founders in 2026, that assumption is wrong. The AI App Studio Cost Paradigm AI app builders have created a fundamentally different cost structure: Build Path Typical Cost AI app builder (subscription) $5 to $300/month Freelancer team $10,000 to $50,000 Agency $40,000 to $400,000+ Industry research suggests companies can report up to 70% cost savings by switching to low-code or AI-powered platforms. While a traditionally coded prototype might still cost $15,000 to $30,000, AI-native platforms allow you to build functional versions for under $1,000 in platform fees. This isn’t about replacing every type of development. Complex enterprise apps with deep regulatory requirements still need traditional teams. But for MVP validation, solo founders testing an idea, and iOS-first products that need to get to market fast, the math has changed completely. Explore x1 pricing tiers to see how a native iOS AI studio compares to traditional development costs. When Traditional Development Still Makes Sense Traditional development is worth the cost when you need: Complex backend systems with custom infrastructure Regulatory compliance (HIPAA, SOC 2, PCI DSS) Enterprise-grade scalability from day one Deep integrations with legacy systems A large cross-functional team coordinating across platforms When an AI Studio Is the Smarter Path An AI app studio fits better when you’re: Validating an MVP before committing serious capital A solo founder or small team with limited budget Building iOS-first and want native Swift/SwiftUI output Prioritizing speed to market over feature breadth Iterating rapidly based on user feedback For non-technical founders especially, the gap between “idea” and “App Store” has narrowed dramatically. The cost question is no longer just “how much does an agency charge?” It’s “which build path fits my stage, budget, and timeline?” If you’re exploring this route, understanding the different types of AI app builders is a useful first step. Today, a single person can launch AI-powered apps that used to demand a large team and a six-figure budget. That reality makes the traditional app cost calculator formula, hours times rate plus PM buffer, feel like it’s measuring the wrong thing for a significant chunk of builders. How to Use an App Cost Calculator Effectively Despite their limitations, calculators aren’t useless. They just need to be used correctly. Step 1: Run Multiple Calculators Use two or three calculators from agencies in different regions. This gives you rate variance and helps you understand how geography affects pricing. If one calculator says $40,000 and another says $120,000 for the same feature set, the difference is almost entirely in the hourly rate assumption. Step 2: Add Your Hidden Cost Buffer Take whatever number you get and add 30 to 40%. This accounts for QA, infrastructure, app store fees, and early post-launch maintenance that calculators don’t model. If the calculator says $80,000, budget $104,000 to $112,000. Step 3: Cross-Check with Discovery Calls The discovery engagement is the step most founders skip because it feels like spending money before spending money. Agencies typically charge $3,000 to $15,000 for a proper discovery phase. It’s also the step that converts a 40% accurate calculator estimate into a 10 to 15% accurate quote with a scope document attached. If three agency quotes cluster around a similar range, your calculator estimate was probably reasonable. If they’re significantly higher, the calculator missed complexity that only a human review could catch. Step 4: Question Whether You Need the Traditional Build Path Before committing to a $50,000+ project, ask whether your v1 actually requires it. Many founders discover that a no-code or AI app builder can get their MVP to market for a fraction of the cost, letting them validate demand before investing in a full custom build. Step 5: Factor in Total Cost of Ownership A calculator gives you the build cost. Your real cost includes: Year one maintenance (potentially 50% of build cost) Ongoing maintenance (15 to 25% annually after that) Server and infrastructure costs (scaling with users) Marketing and user acquisition ($2 to $5 cost per install) Feature iterations based on user feedback The build is just the beginning. The total cost of ownership over three years can be three to five times the initial development estimate. See how x1 works from idea to App Store to understand what a subscription-based build path looks like in practice. Cost Category Year 1 Year 2 Year 3 Development ✔ Maintenance ✔ ✔ ✔ Hosting ✔ ✔ ✔ AI APIs ✔ ✔ ✔ Marketing ✔ ✔ ✔ Feature Updates ✔ ✔ ✔ Which Build Path Is Right for You? If You Are... Best Choice Solo founder AI app studio Startup validating idea AI builder Enterprise Agency Healthcare Traditional development Fintech Traditional development Internal business app Low-code The Bottom Line App cost calculators serve a purpose. They give you a rough sense of what traditional app development costs in 2026, typically $80,000 to $250,000 for a production-ready v1. But they reflect a specific build model (agency or freelance teams billing hourly) and consistently miss 30 to 40% of your actual costs. The more important question for founders in 2026 isn’t “what does my app cost?” It’s “which build path makes sense for my stage?” For complex, regulated, enterprise-grade applications, traditional development remains the right choice, and calculators are a decent starting point for budgeting. For MVP validation, iOS-first products, and solo founders working with limited capital, AI app studios offer a fundamentally different cost structure that most calculators don’t even attempt to model. The smartest move is using calculators for directional awareness while staying clear-eyed about what they can’t tell you. Start building with x1 and see what’s possible at a fraction of traditional development cost. How Long Does It Take to Build an App? App Complexity Typical Timeline MVP 4–8 weeks Medium app 3–6 months Large product 6–12 months Enterprise platform 12–18 months Frequently Asked Questions How much does it cost to build an app in 2026? The average cost for a mid-market mobile app with custom UI, backend APIs, authentication, and analytics is roughly $80,000 to $120,000 through traditional development. Simple MVPs start around $15,000 to $60,000, while complex enterprise apps can exceed $500,000. AI app studios offer an alternative path starting at $5 to $300 per month for subscription-based building. How accurate are app cost calculators? Traditional dropdown-style calculators are typically off by 30 to 50%. AI-powered calculators that draw on large datasets of completed projects can get within 5 to 10% of actual costs when you provide precise inputs. Either way, treat the output as a ballpark, not a budget. What costs do app cost calculators miss? The biggest blind spots are annual maintenance (15 to 25% of build cost per year), first-year post-launch costs (up to 50% of the initial build), compliance and security ($10,000 to $50,000), App Store commissions (up to 30%), and user acquisition marketing. Adding 30 to 40% to any calculator estimate is a practical buffer. Is it cheaper to build for iOS or Android? iOS app development typically ranges from $30,000 to $250,000, while Android ranges from $35,000 to $280,000 (slightly higher due to device fragmentation). Cross-platform frameworks can reduce costs to 50 to 75% of building two native apps, but with tradeoffs in performance and platform-specific polish. Can I build an app for under $1,000? In 2026, yes, if you use an AI app builder or no-code platform. While a traditionally coded prototype still costs $15,000 to $30,000 minimum, AI-native platforms let you build functional versions for under $1,000 in platform fees. The tradeoff is that highly complex or regulated apps still require traditional development resources. Should I hire developers from a cheaper region to save money? Developer rates vary dramatically by region, from $25 to $60 per hour in South and Southeast Asia to $100 to $200 in North America. Cheaper rates can reduce costs significantly, but communication overhead, timezone gaps, and quality variance can erode those savings. Many founders find that running a calculator with different regional rates helps them understand the tradeoff before making a decision. What’s the difference between an app cost calculator and an agency quote? A calculator uses generic feature-to-hours lookup tables and fixed rate assumptions. An agency quote comes after a discovery phase (typically $3,000 to $15,000) where someone reviews your specific requirements, data model, integration needs, and edge cases. The agency quote is usually 10 to 15% accurate. The calculator is a starting point for the conversation that leads to that quote. Do app cost calculators account for AI features? Most don’t. Adding AI capabilities like recommendation engines ($15,000 to $40,000), chatbots ($8,000 to $20,000), or custom ML models ($50,000+) increases costs substantially. In 2026, users increasingly expect AI-powered features as standard, so these costs should be part of your planning even if the calculator doesn’t include them.

title: Civil Liberties Groups File Amicus Brief Opposing NYPD’s Illegal, Secret Seizure and Storage of DNA
summary: For more than a decade, New York City has been amassing the DNA samples of New Yorkers without their consent or any court involvement, as a routine...
body_text: Civil Liberties Groups File Amicus Brief Opposing NYPD’s Illegal, Secret Seizure and Storage of DNA For more than a decade, New York City has been amassing the DNA samples of New Yorkers without their consent or any court involvement, as a routine matter, specifically for inclusion in its “Suspect Index” database Case : Leslie v. City of New York Affiliate : ACLU of New York July 30, 2026 12:00 am ACLU Affiliate New York Civil Liberties Union Spokesperson Vera Eidelman › ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project Media Contact media@aclu.org (212) 549-2666 125 Broad Street 18th Floor New York, NY 10004 United States NEW YORK – Today, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), the New York Civil Liberties Union (NYCLU), and the Cato Institute filed an amicus brief with the Second Circuit in Leslie v. City of New York , in support of The Legal Aid Society’s class action challenge to New York City’s “Suspect DNA Index.” The brief argues that the Suspect Index is a massive and unlawful DNA database. It also emphasizes that DNA contains an individual’s highly sensitive and private information, and that DNA that people inevitably leave on items they discard—from a used cup to a cigarette butt to a tissue—cannot be seized, searched, and stored without a warrant. The Suspect Index contains DNA samples from more than 34,000 people, including kids and people who have never been charged with a crime. Many of the samples are gathered through the NYPD’s practice of collecting DNA by arresting individuals for purported crimes, holding them for many hours, bringing them into an interrogation room specifically cleaned and set up to collect their DNA, pressuring them to drink or touch something, and concluding the interview as soon as that’s done. The NYPD then leads the individuals out in handcuffs (such that they cannot take whatever they touched or consumed even if they wanted to) and then goes back in to obtain the item specifically to extract the unavoidably shed DNA. “For more than a decade, the NYPD has been operating a rogue DNA database not authorized by law,” said Beth Haroules, director of disability justice litigation at the NYCLU. “No New Yorker should have their DNA taken illegally and stored in a secret database. This destructive practice disproportionately targets Black and brown New Yorkers and violates our Fourth Amendment rights. No court should allow this intrusion on our privacy.” “The government cannot treat our DNA like it treats our garbage, and seize, search, and store it without a warrant,” said Vera Eidelman, senior staff attorney at the ACLU’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project . “Usually we rely on hypotheticals to highlight the dystopian possibilities of this kind of privacy invasion, but no hypothetical could be more troubling than New York City’s actual practice: amassing thousands of people’s DNA without their knowledge, their consent, or any court-ordered or legislative guardrails. If the Second Circuit does not intervene, all I can say is: New Yorkers, hold on to your trash.” The brief argues that the Suspect Index violates state law, which establishes a separate state databank as the only DNA index that can exist in New York and sets strict limits on whose DNA can be collected, when, for what purpose, and when it has to be deleted—all of which the Suspect Index ignores. The Index also includes samples from people who have been expressly excluded as suspects in a crime, arrestees who have never been convicted of a crime, and exonerated or acquitted individuals. “The secret, dragnet collection of DNA for inclusion on a 'Suspect Index' sounds dystopian. Yet it's an affront to privacy and the presumption of innocence tens of thousands of New Yorkers have already suffered. The Fourth Amendment protects against this—and hopefully, so will the Second Circuit,” said Matthew Cavedon, Director of the Project on Criminal Justice at the Cato Institute . A copy of the brief can be found here . New York Jul 2026 Privacy & Technology Leslie v. City of New York Status: Ongoing Explore case Leslie V. City Of New York. Explore Case.
